panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Upper photograph of the same newborn showing a closed/drooping left upper eyelid with the right eye open; the caption and in-text describe left-sided ptosis with the lid opening below the upper eyelid margin, matching the configured finding of unilateral congenital ptosis. Disease attribution is supported by the disease-focused article title (neonatal diagnosis of Marcus Gunn jaw-winking syndrome) plus a specific captioned manifestation. Newborn is described in text, so age_group is child (no infant option). B: Lower photograph of the same newborn, closer view of both eyes, showing persistent left upper eyelid ptosis (reduced palpebral aperture) with a normal-appearing right eye, corresponding to the captioned left-sided ptosis of Marcus Gunn jaw-winking syndrome. No jaw-winking (dynamic retraction on sucking/chewing) is demonstrated in this static image, so only the ptosis finding is tagged.

in_text_mentions: erformed soon after birth, left‐eye ptosis was observed without evidence of edema. Namely, the newborn was hardly able to lift his left eyelid, whose opening was below the upper eyelid margin (Figure 1). Pupils were bilaterally isochoric, isocyclic, and reactive to light. Newborn's general appearance and clinical conditions were otherwise normal. No nervous system anomalies were detected. At 3 days of life, a first ophthalmologist evaluation was performed, and possible congenital ptosis was suspected. The red reflex test was normal. Brain sonography excluded abnormalities. panels.rationale: The figure is a clinical photograph of a patient presenting with ptosis. The associated article title and text explicitly link this condition to Marcus Gunn Jaw-Winking Syndrome, fulfilling the inclusion criteria.
panels.attribution_text: Saldanha and Daigavane. Marcus Gunn Jaw-Winking Phenomenon and Monocular Elevation Deficiency in Association With Congenital Ptosis.. Cureus 2023. doi:10.7759/cureus.33817. CC BY (https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/). Figure 1.
panels.figure_caption: Clinical image showing severe congenital ptosis in the left eye.
in_text_mentions: aperture's height was 2 mm in the left eye and 10 mm in the right. The levator palpebrae superioris (LPS) function test results for the right eye were normal (15 mm) and that for the left eye was poor (3 mm), both with good Bell's phenomenon. The patient's ptosis improved when she moved her jaw to the right side (normal side), and her eyelid opened to about 8 mm. However, when she moved her jaw to the left, her eyelid did not change (Figures 1-2). Extraocular muscle movements showed restriction in dextroelevation and levoelevation in the left eye. Ice pack test showed no improvement in ptosis.

plate_findings.evidence: The left eye exhibits significantly greater ptosis compared to the right eye (3 mm palpebral fissure height vs 8 mm).
Ptosis is evident, though the text notes ptosis improved significantly when he opened his mouth, illustrating the jaw-winking synkinesis.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 2 panels (A, B). A: Panel A shows a patient at rest exhibiting asymmetric ptosis (specifically more pronounced in the left eye), a classic presentation of MGJWS. B: Panel B shows the patient during active jaw movement, illustrating the jaw-winking synkinesis associated with MGJWS, where the ptosis is altered or improved with jaw movement.

in_text_mentions: revealed a palpebral fissure height of 8 mm in the right eye and 3 mm in the left, with marginal reflex distance (MRD) measurements of +3 mm in the right eye and -2 mm in the left. Notably, the patient’s ptosis improved significantly when he opened his mouth, as illustrated in Figure 1. Upward gaze in the left eye was also restricted in all gaze positions, as shown in Figure 2. No evidence of esotropia or epiblepharon was observed on examination. Given the patient’s restricted upward gaze and ptosis that improved with jaw movement, these findings were suggestive of MGJWS with accompanying MED.
